newsitem.title: ITALY: Venice prize goes to IRA film "Michael Collins".
newsitem.headline: Venice prize goes to IRA film "Michael Collins".

text.p: The Venice Film Festival awarded its Golden Lion prize for best film to "Michael Collins," the controversial IRA movie by Dublin-born director Neil Jordan.

Jordan, who has already come under attack by politicians in Britian who fear the film will contribute to sectarian tensions in Northern Ireland, said he hoped its release in Britain early next year would have the opposite effect.
"All I want is for everything to be peaceful," he told a news conference in Venice after accepting the festival's top prize on Saturday night.
Asked whether he believed the film would help the peace process, Jordan replied: "I made it with that hope in mind because of the history of my country".

But Jordan, whose 1992 film "The Crying Game" also came under fire for what was perceived as a sympathetic portrayal of the Irish Republican Army, added, "Once you put a gun in a situation, it is very difficult to take it out again".
Liam Neeson, who plays the lead in the film, took the Golden Lion prize for best actor.
Neeson was not able to accept the award as he was still in hospital in nearby Padua after falling ill with an intestinal problem earlier in the festival.

Aidan Quinn, Neeson's supporting actor in "Michael Collins", accepted the award on his behalf and said Neeson was "deeply honoured" to receive the award and was happy with "the fantastic audiences at Venice who received the film so enthusiastically".

The film recounts the life of Michael Collins, the IRA's former director of intelligence who helped fight for Ireland's independence from 1919 to 1921. Collins was killed in an IRA ambush in 1922 after breaking with his comrades when he sought a negotiated settlement with Britain.

"Studios usually don't make movies that show at festivals like this, particularly movies which deal with difficult subjects that can give rise to arguments of all kind," Jordan said in his acceptance speech.
"I felt that "Michael Collins' would make a good movie, especially for Ireland," he said.
The Warner Bros production which also stars Julia Roberts, was chosen from a field of 17 films competing at the 11-day Venice festival.
The nine-member jury at this year's festival was headed by director Roman Polanski and included writer Paul Aster, actress Anjelica Houston and Indian director Mrinal Sen.
The Golden Lion award for best actress went to four-year-old French actress Victoire Thivisol, who played the leading role in director Jacques Doillon's film "Ponette".

Thivisol plays a girl who tries to deal with the unbearable absence of her mother who is killed in a car accident. She looks for her and waits for her and no one can convince her her mother will not return.

Doillon, in accepting the award for Thivisol, referred to the fact that some people in the audience at the film's screening earlier this week booed at the end and said they disapproved of the use of such a young actress.
"Victoire did not make this film under threats," Doillon said.

Actor Chris Penn was awarded the best supporting actor prize for his role in American director Abel Ferrara's "The Funeral" in which he portrays a young mob member out to avenge his brother's killing.

A special jury award was given to "Brigands" by Georgian- born director Otar Iosseliani and Britian's Ken Loach received a special medal for a film devoted to human solidarity for "Carla's Song", a love story with a political background set in Nicaragua in the late 1980s.
Golden Lion prizes for lifetime achievement were awarded to Italian actor Vittorio Gassman, French actress Michele Morgan and American director Robert Altmam.
Dustin Hoffman, who could not be present on Saturday night, had been awarded a lifetime achievement prize earlier in the festival.
